Outlying islands in Southeast Alaska stay restocked with deer that way. Probably every island of any size will have deer, but there are big ones that don't have wolves. Wolves are abundant in southern and mainland Southeast. They can swim too, but they don't appear to be able to catch a swimming deer. I have seen a wolf standing on the beach looking longingly after a deer that had escaped it by getting to the water and swimming away. Even though deer will happily take to water, they seem to think the better of it when they are offered a ride while while swimming. I have heard many accounts of boaters picking up swimming deer. The show must go on and, in the end, you see that you did fine.

Remember, if you can't play your instrument - play the audience. Of course, it's best to play 'em both but they're both there to be played. Getting the audience involved is sometimes the best option you have.

At the same time, inviting people on stage CAN have some risks associated with it. But, a good soundbooth is ready to mute 'em or turn them down.

I am the sound booth guy! I had the PA right behind me on a shelf, so I could make changes to the sound pretty easily.

It turned out real good. I stayed there and talked to most of the people there afterwards for an hour or so after I was done playing. Nearly everybody there seemed to want to come up and talk to me and tell me how much they enjoyed it. That was really cool.

The audiences usually love to be involved - more so at small venues. They're there to have a good time. They want to have a good time. They'll go out of their way to make sure they have a good time. Getting them involved is a way to enable them to have fun. You're there to provide more than music - you're there to enable 'em to have a good time.

So, sometimes you'll play them just as much (if not more) than you'll play your instruments. It helps to get comfortable interacting with the crowd. I find some people have a hard time with that, but it just takes some confidence. I typically refer to it as 'bantering with the audience.' It's a part of every show that I do, though how much of a part it is will vary per show.

There's a lot of need to be dynamic. Shows are all different, crowds are all different, and venues are all different. In your case, I'm sure there's a lot of familiar faces and you're used to the venue as that's the only place you really perform in front of paying customers. But, you'll still want to be dynamic - to go with the flow of things, to keep things different, to keep things changing with the audience's experiences.

It's an art form in and of itself. These skills also help in other areas of your life. They'll help you give presentations, speak with clients, have confidence in social gatherings, and even pick up chicks! Not that you need help with picking up chicks, but it's a great skill to have.
